claim: E. coli colonies grown on M9 minimal medium display two growth phases: exponential growth in volume, height, and diameter for up to ~24 hr, followed by linear growth.
source: Colonies generally displayed two growth phases: colonies showed exponential growth in volume, height, and diameter for up to ~24 hr, followed by linear growth (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of colony morphology over time shown in Figure 1A and B, which display cross-sectional profiles and quantitative measurements of volume, radius, and height.

claim: The transition in colony growth dynamics around 24 hr has previously been hypothesized to be caused by a change in metabolism due to altered nutrient penetration and consumption for colonies above a certain size.
source: This transition in colony growth dynamics has previously been observed, and was hypothesized to be caused by a change in metabolism due to altered nutrient penetration and consumption for colonies above a certain size (Pirt, 1967; Warren et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Pirt (1967) and Warren et al. (2019) that proposed this hypothesis.

claim: Whole-colony transcriptomes revealed a major change after 24 hr of growth.
source: The transcriptomes revealed a major change after 24 hr of growth (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1C, which displays expression profiles of 4231 genes during colony growth.

claim: After 72 hr of growth, 966 out of 4231 detected genes were differentially expressed in comparison to the 12 hr time point.
source: After 72 hr of growth, 966 out of 4231 detected genes were differentially expressed in comparison to the 12 hr time point (log2-fold-changes > 1 or <-1, and FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: Biofilm matrix biosynthesis genes are expressed continuously during colony growth.
source: The whole-colony transcriptomes also showed that biofilm matrix biosynthesis genes are expressed continuously during colony growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, which displays expression of genes involved in cellulose, curli, colanic acid, and PGA production.

claim: E. coli extracellular matrix is composed of cellulose, curli, colanic acid, β–1,6-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (PGA) and flagella.
source: E. coli extracellular matrix is composed of cellulose, curli, colanic acid, β–1,6-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (PGA) and flagella (Hobley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Hobley et al., 2015 as the source of this information.

claim: Mixed acid fermentation and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle pathways were differentially regulated after 24 hr of growth.
source: Furthermore, the transcriptomes confirmed that well-known pathways such as mixed acid fermentation and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle were differentially regulated after 24 hr of growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,C, which displays fold-changes of genes involved in these pathways.

claim: Above a certain colony size, which is reached between 24 and 32 hr, the consumption of oxygen by cells in the outer region of the colony causes a large anoxic region inside the colony.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that above a certain colony size, which is reached between 24 and 32 hr in our conditions, the consumption of oxygen by cells in the outer region of the colony causes a large anoxic region inside the colony.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from transcriptomic data showing differential regulation of anaerobic and aerobic pathways, and is consistent with the observed growth transition.

claim: The gene coding for the alanine exporter AlaE showed strong expression changes (~50 fold increase) in 72-hr-colonies relative to 12-hr-colonies.
source: Interestingly, the gene coding for the alanine exporter AlaE (Hori et al., 2011b) showed strong expression changes (~50 fold increase) in 72-hr-colonies relative to 12-hr-colonies (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1D, which displays mean expression fold-changes of amino acid exporters during colony growth.

claim: All amino acid abundances decreased during colony growth except for alanine, which remained relatively constant with a peak abundance at 32 hr.
source: All amino acid abundances decreased during colony growth – except for alanine, which remained relatively constant with a peak abundance at 32 hr (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry measurements of amino acid profiles shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: mRuby2 fluorescence is a reliable indicator of oxygen levels in E. coli colonies.
source: By using an oxygen microsensor to directly measure oxygen levels inside the colony in the z-direction (Jo et al., 2017), we determined that the mRuby2 fluorescence was a reliable indicator of oxygen levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct comparison of mRuby2 fluorescence measurements with oxygen microsensor measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of the colony became non-fluorescent (i.e. anoxic) around 24 hr.
source: During colony growth, the fraction of fluorescent cells in the colony decreased (inset in Figure 2B), and the majority of the colony became non-fluorescent (i.e. anoxic) around 24 hr, which coincides with the time at which the whole-colony transcriptome shifted towards anaerobic metabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mRuby2 fluorescence over time shown in the inset of Figure 2B, and is consistent with transcriptomic data.

claim: Chromophore maturation of mRuby2 is oxygen-dependent.
source: The method is based on the oxygen-dependence of chromophore maturation of the fluorescent protein mRuby2 (Lam et al., 2012; Tsien, 1998).
evidence: The claim cites Lam et al., 2012 and Tsien, 1998 as sources for the oxygen-dependence of mRuby2 chromophore maturation.

claim: The expression of the alanine exporter gene alaE was significantly upregulated in the inner (non-fluorescent) region of the colony, compared with the outer (fluorescent) region.
source: In particular, the spatial transcriptomes showed that the expression of the alanine exporter gene alaE was significantly upregulated in the inner (non-fluorescent) region of the colony, compared with the outer (fluorescent) region (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial transcriptome data shown in Figure 2E, which displays fold-changes between inner and outer regions of 72 hr colonies.

claim: The dadAX operon was down-regulated in the inner region, compared with the outer region in colonies grown for 72 hr.
source: In colonies grown for 72 hr, the dadAX operon was down-regulated in the inner region, compared with the outer region (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial transcriptome data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The dadAX operon encodes a racemase (dadX) and a dehydrogenase (dadA).
source: The latter encodes a racemase (dadX) and a dehydrogenase (dadA) (Lobocka et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim cites Lobocka et al., 1994 as the source for the function of dadAX operon genes.

claim: Alanine is only secreted under anoxic conditions with glucose and ammonium.
source: Mass spectrometry measurements from culture supernatants clearly showed that alanine is only secreted under anoxic conditions with glucose and ammonium (Figure 3A), which is an environment that corresponds to the anoxic base of the colony, where cells are in contact with the glucose- and ammonium-rich M9 agar.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry measurements of extracellular alanine in different growth conditions shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Oxic conditions with abundant glucose and ammonium did not result in significant alanine secretion.
source: Oxic conditions with abundant glucose and ammonium did not result in significant alanine secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: E. coli can use extracellular alanine as a carbon or nitrogen source in oxic conditions.
source: It is well-known that E. coli can use extracellular alanine as a carbon or nitrogen source in oxic conditions (Franklin and Venables, 1976; Kornberg, 1965), which we confirmed for our strain and growth conditions by replacing either glucose or ammonium with alanine in the liquid shaking M9 medium (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Franklin and Venables, 1976 and Kornberg, 1965, and confirmed by growth curve data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Exogenous alanine can be utilized as a poor carbon source, but as a good nitrogen source in oxic conditions.
source: We found that exogenous alanine can be utilized as a poor carbon source, but as a good nitrogen source in oxic conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Under anoxic conditions, E. coli cannot utilize alanine as a carbon or nitrogen source.
source: Interestingly, we observed that under anoxic conditions, E. coli cannot utilize alanine as a carbon or nitrogen source (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optical density measurements after 96 hr of incubation in anoxic conditions shown in Figure 3D.

claim: None of the deletions of alanine transport and degradation genes affected the cellular growth rates in liquid culture.
source: None of these deletions affected the cellular growth rates in liquid culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletions of alanine transport and degradation genes did not cause clear phenotypes in colony height or diameter after 72 hr of incubation on M9 agar.
source: These deletions also did not cause clear phenotypes in colony height or diameter after 72 hr of incubation on M9 agar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that alanine export and consumption do not have large effects on global colony size.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of colony diameter and height shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Colonies carrying the ΔalaEΔdadAX deletion displayed increased cell death in the oxic region at around 50% of the maximum colony height.
source: We observed that the colonies displayed only a low fraction of dead cells at the bottom edges of the colony, but cell death increased towards the top of the colony. Interestingly, the oxic region at around 50 % of the maximum colony height displayed increased cell death when cells carried the ΔalaEΔdadAX deletion (Figure 4A), which is a strain that should have a strongly reduced capability for secreting and consuming alanine.
evidence: The claim is supported by SYTOX Green fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutants incapable of the major alanine degradation pathway (ΔdadAX) displayed substantially higher extracellular alanine than cells that are impaired for alanine secretion as well (ΔalaEΔdadAX).
source: As expected, mutants incapable of the major alanine degradation pathway (ΔdadAX) displayed substantially higher extracellular alanine than cells that are impaired for alanine secretion as well (ΔalaEΔdadAX).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry measurements of extracellular alanine shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AlaE acts as an alanine exporter inside colonies.
source: Amino acid transporters can often function as both importers and exporters, yet the higher extracellular alanine levels of the ΔdadAX strain compared with the ΔalaEΔdadAX strain (Figure 4B) indicate that AlaE acts as an alanine exporter inside colonies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data comparing extracellular alanine levels in different mutants shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AlaE acts as an exporter in liquid cultures.
source: Previous measurements have shown that AlaE also acts as an exporter in liquid cultures (Hori et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim cites Hori et al., 2011b as the source for this information.

claim: Another mechanism for alanine export might exist that is currently unknown.
source: Interestingly, and consistent with the results of Hori et al. in liquid cultures (Hori et al., 2011a; Hori et al., 2011b), our detection of extracellular alanine in colonies of the ΔalaE and ΔalaEΔdadAX mutants indicates that another mechanism for alanine export might exist that is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data showing extracellular alanine in ΔalaE mutants, and is consistent with previous work by Hori et al.

claim: Excess levels of intracellular alanine can inhibit growth.
source: It has previously been shown that excess levels of intracellular alanine can inhibit growth (Katsube et al., 2019), yet the molecular mechanism underlying this process is still unclear.
evidence: The claim cites Katsube et al., 2019 as the source for this information.

claim: All strains show a decreased growth rate in liquid media containing high levels of alanine.
source: Indeed, we observed that all strains show a decreased growth rate in liquid media containing high levels of alanine, yet strains carrying the ΔalaEΔdadAX mutation were much more sensitive to exogenously added alanine than the parental strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements as a function of alanine concentration shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Strains carrying the ΔalaEΔdadAX mutation were much more sensitive to exogenously added alanine than the parental strain.
source: Indeed, we observed that all strains show a decreased growth rate in liquid media containing high levels of alanine, yet strains carrying the ΔalaEΔdadAX mutation were much more sensitive to exogenously added alanine than the parental strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The parental strain did not display increased levels of cell death when exposed to extracellular alanine.
source: We found that even though the parental strain displayed a reduced growth rate when exposed to extracellular alanine (Figure 4C), the parental strain did not display increased levels of cell death in such conditions (Figure 4D) – likely due to their ability to secrete and consume alanine, allowing them to control their intracellular levels of alanine.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the presence of high extracellular alanine concentrations, ΔalaEΔdadAX mutants displayed higher cell death levels than the parental strain, which was particularly strong in stationary phase conditions.
source: In contrast, we found that in the presence of high extracellular alanine concentrations, ΔalaEΔdadAX mutants displayed higher cell death levels than the parental strain, which was particularly strong in stationary phase conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ΔalaEΔdadAX mutant was consistently strongly outcompeted by the parental strain during colony growth.
source: We also observed that the ΔalaEΔdadAX mutant was consistently strongly outcompeted by the parental strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B), despite having no liquid culture grow differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and regardless of the fluorescent protein that they were carrying.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Cells capable of alanine cross-feeding have a fitness advantage during colony growth.
source: These experiments indicate that cells capable of alanine cross-feeding have a fitness advantage during colony growth.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from competition experiment data.

claim: ΔalaEΔdadAX and ΔalaE mutants displayed a significantly decreased colony curvature in the mid-height region, in comparison to the parental strain.
source: Measurements of the colony morphology showed that ΔalaEΔdadAX and ΔalaE mutants displayed a significantly decreased colony curvature in the relevant region, in comparison to the parental strain (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony morphology measurements shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The parental strain grows faster in the mid-height oxic region than the cross-feeding impaired ΔalaEΔdadAX mutant.
source: These measurements showed that the parental strain grows faster in the mid-height oxic region than the cross-feeding impaired ΔalaEΔdadAX mutant (Figure 5C), which further supports the hypothesis that this region of the colony relies on alanine as a carbon and nitrogen source.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of the fluorescence ratio of unstable GFP and mRuby2 shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells at the bottom periphery of 72 hr colonies have access to oxygen, glucose, and ammonium, and perform either aerobic respiration or fermentation by overflow metabolism.
source: Cells at the bottom periphery of the colony (red region in Figure 6A) have access to oxygen, glucose, and ammonium, and perform either aerobic respiration or fermentation by overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Cole et al., 2015) – these two possible metabolic states cannot be distinguished with our current approaches.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from spatial transcriptome and metabolome data, and cites Basan et al., 2015 and Cole et al., 2015 for the concept of overflow metabolism.

claim: Cells at the bottom center of 72 hr colonies are anaerobic yet they have access to glucose and ammonium from the agar-solidified medium.
source: Cells at the bottom center of the colony (orange region in Figure 6A) are anaerobic yet they have access to glucose and ammonium from the agar-solidified medium.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from spatial transcriptome data and oxygen measurements.

claim: Cells at the bottom center of 72 hr colonies ferment glucose and secrete alanine, primarily via AlaE.
source: These cells ferment glucose and secrete alanine, primarily via AlaE.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from spatial transcriptome data showing upregulation of alaE in the inner region, and mass spectrometry data showing alanine secretion under anoxic conditions with glucose and ammonium.

claim: Secreted alanine diffuses through the colony and can only be utilized by oxic nutrient-deprived cells.
source: Secreted alanine diffuses through the colony and can only be utilized by oxic nutrient-deprived cells (blue region in Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from spatial transcriptome data showing upregulation of dadAX in the outer region, and growth experiments showing alanine can only be utilized as a carbon/nitrogen source in oxic conditions.

claim: Alanine consumption in the mid-height oxic region has a detoxification effect, by reducing otherwise inhibitory levels of extracellular alanine.
source: Alanine consumption in the mid-height oxic region also has a detoxification effect, by reducing otherwise inhibitory levels of extracellular alanine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing that high extracellular alanine inhibits growth and increases cell death in ΔalaEΔdadAX mutants.

claim: Alanine secretion in the anaerobic base of the colony may be a necessity to avoid high intracellular alanine levels that presumably result from anaerobic fermentation of glucose in the presence of ammonium.
source: We speculate that this is not an altruistic trait evolved to support a starving oxic subpopulation at a different location, because such a trait would be highly susceptible to social cheaters in a multi-species community. Instead, alanine secretion in this region may be a necessity to avoid high intracellular alanine levels that presumably result from anaerobic fermentation of glucose in the presence of ammonium.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that high alanine levels are inhibitory.

claim: The presence of the alanine-consuming subpopulation results in a benefit for the alanine-secreting subpopulation, by causing a higher diffusive flux of alanine away from the alanine-secreting population.
source: On the other side of the cross-feeding interaction, the alanine-consuming subpopulation in the aerobic mid-height region of the colony strongly benefits from the secreted alanine originating from the base of the colony. We note that the alanine consumption in the aerobic mid-height region of the colony necessarily causes a steeper alanine concentration gradient between the two interacting subpopulations, compared with a case in which no alanine is consumed. Due to Fick's law of diffusion, a steeper concentration gradient causes a higher diffusive flux. Therefore, the presence of the alanine-consuming subpopulation results in a benefit for the alanine-secreting subpopulation, by causing a higher diffusive flux of alanine away from the alanine-secreting population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established physical principles (Fick's law of diffusion) applied to the observed alanine cross-feeding.

claim: The interaction between the two cross-feeding subpopulations is likely mutualistic.
source: In summary, the interaction between the two cross-feeding subpopulations is likely mutualistic.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that both subpopulations benefit from the cross-feeding interaction.

claim: The spatial organization of alanine cross-feeding between two subpopulations is analogous to the carbon cross-feeding in E. coli colonies via acetate.
source: The spatial organization of alanine cross-feeding between two subpopulations we described in this study is analogous to the carbon cross-feeding in E. coli colonies via acetate, because it involves metabolite secretion in the anaerobic population and consumption in the carbon-starved oxic population (Cole et al., 2015; Dal Co et al., 2019; Wolfsberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim compares the observed alanine cross-feeding to previously described acetate cross-feeding, citing Cole et al., 2015, Dal Co et al., 2019, and Wolfsberg et al., 2018.

claim: The location of the population that is proposed to consume acetate as a carbon source spans most of the oxic region of the colony.
source: However, the location of the population that is proposed to consume acetate as a carbon source spans most of the oxic region of the colony (Cole et al., 2015), whereas alanine is primarily consumed only in the oxic mid-height region of the colony.
evidence: The claim cites Cole et al., 2015 for the location of acetate consumption, and contrasts it with the observed location of alanine consumption.

claim: Spatial transcriptomes did not reveal a signature for acetate cross-feeding between the anaerobic and oxic regions of the colony.
source: Interestingly, our spatial transcriptomes did not reveal a signature for acetate cross-feeding between the anaerobic and oxic regions of the colony (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), yet transcripts coding for enzymes involved in lactate, formate, and succinate metabolism display patterns that are indicative of spatially organized metabolism that could be the basis of carbon cross-feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of spatial transcriptome data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Alanine can be shared in colonies of the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis, and this effect required three-dimensional colonies for unknown reasons.
source: Very recently, it was shown that alanine can be shared in colonies of the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis, and that this effect required three-dimensional colonies for unknown reasons (Arjes et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Arjes et al., 2021 as the source for this information.

claim: In E. coli, three-dimensional growth is required to create an anoxic region replete with carbon and nitrogen sources that causes alanine secretion.
source: In our E. coli model system, three-dimensional growth is required to create an anoxic region replete with carbon and nitrogen sources that causes alanine secretion, and we speculate that this effect may also be required in B. subtilis, and in other species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed requirement for anoxic conditions with glucose and ammonium for alanine secretion, and speculation about other species.

claim: Biofilms are estimated to be the most abundant form of microbial life on Earth.
source: Such spatially structured assemblages, called biofilms (Flemming et al., 2016), are estimated to be the most abundant form of microbial life on Earth (Flemming and Wuertz, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Flemming and Wuertz, 2019 as the source for this estimate.

claim: The metabolic activity of cells inside biofilms leads to spatial gradients of oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen sources, as well as many other nutrients and waste products.
source: The metabolic activity of cells inside these dense populations leads to spatial gradients of oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen sources, as well as many other nutrients and waste products (Ackermann, 2015; Evans et al., 2020; Pacheco et al., 2019; Stewart and Franklin, 2008).
evidence: The claim cites Ackermann, 2015, Evans et al., 2020, Pacheco et al., 2019, and Stewart and Franklin, 2008 as sources for this information.

claim: Bacterial growth into densely packed spatially structured communities, and metabolic activity of the constituent cells, naturally lead to physiological differentiation.
source: Bacterial growth into densely packed spatially structured communities, and metabolic activity of the constituent cells, therefore naturally lead to physiological differentiation (Evans et al., 2020; Røder et al., 2020; Serra et al., 2013a; Stewart and Franklin, 2008).
evidence: The claim cites Evans et al., 2020, Røder et al., 2020, Serra et al., 2013a, and Stewart and Franklin, 2008 as sources for this information.

claim: Metabolic and phenotypic heterogeneities are frequently observed in multi-species communities.
source: Metabolic and phenotypic heterogeneities are frequently observed in multi-species communities (Garg et al., 2016; Henson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020; Pacheco et al., 2021; Serra and Hengge, 2021) and in single-species biofilm populations (Cole et al., 2015; Dal Co et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2018; Moree et al., 2012; Rani et al., 2007; Serra et al., 2013b; Teal et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources for observations of heterogeneity in both multi-species and single-species communities.

claim: Single-species biofilms offer precisely controllable model systems with reduced complexity for understanding basic mechanisms of metabolic differentiation and the interaction of subpopulations.
source: In contrast, single-species biofilms offer precisely controllable model systems with reduced complexity for understanding basic mechanisms of metabolic differentiation and the interaction of subpopulations.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the advantages of single-species systems compared to multi-species systems.

claim: Investigations of phenotypic heterogeneity in single-species assemblages have revealed fundamental insights into metabolic interactions of subpopulations with consequences for the overall fitness and growth dynamics of the assemblages.
source: Investigations of phenotypic heterogeneity in single-species assemblages have already revealed fundamental insights into metabolic interactions of subpopulations with consequences for the overall fitness and growth dynamics of the assemblages (Arjes et al., 2021; Cole et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015; Wolfsberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources for previous insights from single-species biofilm studies.

claim: The mRuby2 fluorophore maturation time is approximately 150 min.
source: The time between colony disruption and imaging for this control experiment was less than 2 min, which is substantially shorter than the mRuby2 fluorophore maturation time (~150 min Lam et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites Lam et al., 2012 as the source for the mRuby2 maturation time.

claim: Formaldehyde fixation prevents mRuby2 fluorophore maturation in the presence of oxygen without altering the transcriptomes.
source: To obtain spatial transcriptomes, we then separated colonies grown for 72 hr into individual cells, immediately fixed them with formaldehyde (which prevents mRuby2 fluorophore maturation in the presence of oxygen without altering the transcriptomes; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and subjected them to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to separate the oxic (fluorescent) and anoxic (not fluorescent) populations (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strain lacking flagella due to the deletion of the flagellin (ΔfliC) resulted in highly reproducible and axially symmetric colony morphologies.
source: Therefore, a strain lacking flagella due to the deletion of the flagellin (ΔfliC) was used as the parental strain for all following experiments, which resulted in highly reproducible and axially symmetric colony morphologies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The wild-type E. coli strain AR3110 displayed motility on filter membranes on M9 agar, which led to heterogeneous colony development and an asymmetric colony morphology.
source: When we grew E. coli wild-type colonies in these conditions, we observed motility on the filter membranes on M9 agar, which led to heterogeneous colony development and an asymmetric colony morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.
